title: Water table moderates Scots pine growth responses to wood ash fertilization in boreal drained Scots pine peatland forests
content:
Abstract
Nutrient limitations reduce the long-term productivity of boreal drained peatland forests. Wood ash fertilization (AF) can improve nutrient availability, but its interaction with water table (WT) conditions remains insufficiently understood. WT regulates both nutrient and water availability, thereby potentially influencing growth responses induced by AF. We examined the effects of AF on Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) basal area increment (BAI), carbon isotope composition (δ13C), and needle nutrient contents at two drained peatland sites in northern Finland with different WT regimes: shallow WT (July–August mean WT: −26 cm) and deep WT (July–August mean WT: −71 cm). Each site included a Treatment plot, where thinning was conducted in 2009–2010 and granulated wood ash applied in spring 2014 (45 kg P ha−1, 117 kg K ha−1), and a Control plot that received neither thinning nor fertilization. Stand BAI (2005–2022) was estimated from successive stand inventories and tree-ring cores. Annual tree-ring δ13C was analysed for the years 2005–2022, needle nutrient contents were measured annually (2014–2023), and WT was monitored biweekly (2007–2020). AF improved needle nutrient status at both sites. However, increases in needle mass and BAI were substantially greater with the shallow WT and accompanied by less negative tree-ring δ13C values. This suggests increased photosynthetic assimilation relative to stomatal conductance with shallow WT. Improved needle nutrient status in each site did not result in comparable physiological or growth responses indicating that water availability may have constrained the benefits of fertilization. Although causal attribution is limited by the paired-site design and prior thinning, our findings show that AF improves needle nutrient status regardless of WT depth, but tree growth and physiological responses may be constrained by limited water availability. Together, the results support the hypothesis that maintaining growing-season WT shallower than ~−40 cm may enhance the effectiveness of AF in boreal drained Scots pine peatland forests.
